name: Ruth

seo.title: Ruth in the Bible: her story, her vow to Naomi, and Boaz
seo.description: Ruth in plain words: the widow from Moab who would not leave Naomi, the barley field of Boaz, and her place in the family tree of Jesus.

band.lede: A widow from Moab who would not leave her mother-in-law. She gleaned barley in the field of Boaz, married him, and became King David's great-grandmother.

who: Ruth was a woman of Moab who married into a family from Bethlehem. When her husband died, she would not leave her widowed mother-in-law, Naomi. She went home with her to Judah and gleaned barley in the field of Boaz, who married her. Their son Obed was the grandfather of King David.

tidbits.text: Jews read her book at **Shavuot**, the Feast of Weeks, 50 days after Passover. Her story, like the feast, comes at harvest time.

Josephus retold her story around the year 93. In his version, Boaz bids Ruth pull off the other kinsman's shoe and “spit in his face, according to the law”, as Deuteronomy 25:9 lays down. Her own book has the kinsman take off his own sandal.

cite.text: Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, book 5, chapter 9; Ruth 4:8; Deuteronomy 25:9

tidbits.text: An old Jewish tradition in the Talmud says the prophet **Samuel** wrote her book. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1912 already called that groundless. The writer is unknown.
The Law of Moses said no Moabite could enter the assembly of the LORD, “even to the tenth generation.” Yet a woman of Moab became the great-grandmother of King David.

facts.label: In the Bible
facts.text: The book of **Ruth**, four short chapters. Outside it, only **Matthew** 1:5 names her, in the family tree of Jesus.

facts.label: Her book
facts.text: Christian Bibles place it after **Judges**, as the Greek Septuagint did. Hebrew Bibles put it among the **Writings**, as one of five short scrolls.

facts.label: When
facts.text: “In the days when the judges ruled”. Josephus places it in the time of **Eli**, the priest who raised Samuel.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: **Moab**, east of the Dead Sea, where she was born. Then **Bethlehem** in Judah, her husband's family's town.

facts.label: Her name
facts.text: Hebrew **Rut**. Probably from a word for **friendship**.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: Married first to **Mahlon**, Naomi's son, then to **Boaz**. Her son **Obed** was the grandfather of **King David**. Her father and mother are mentioned but never named.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Ruth the Moabitess**, five times in her own book. **Righteous Ruth**, in the Orthodox Church.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: The Bible does not say. In the 1880s, British surveyors at **Hebron** were shown her tomb in a small mosque, beside the traditional tomb of Jesse.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: Painters show her in the harvest field, or pleading with **Naomi** on the road, as at the top of this page.

feasts.note: The **Orthodox** keep her on a Sunday, not a date. The **OCA** lists **Righteous Ruth** on the **Sunday of the Forefathers**, between 11 and 17 December, and names her again on the **Sunday before the Nativity**. The **Catholic** calendar has no day for her.

moments.when: In the days of the judges
moments.title: A family from Bethlehem
moments.text: “In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land.” A man of Bethlehem named Elimelech took his wife Naomi and their two sons to live in Moab. There Elimelech died. His sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. About ten years later both sons died too, and Naomi “was left without her two sons and without her husband.”

moments.title: “Ruth clung to her”
moments.text: Naomi heard that the LORD had given His people food again, and set out for home with both her daughters-in-law. On the road she stopped them. “Go back, each of you to your mother’s home,” she said. She had no more sons for them to marry. They wept aloud. Then “Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth clung to her.” Naomi tried once more. Ruth's answer is below, in her words. “When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped trying to persuade her.”

moments.when: The start of the barley harvest
moments.title: “Call me Mara”
moments.text: The two women walked on to Bethlehem, and the whole town was stirred. “Can this be Naomi?” the women asked. “Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty.” They arrived at the beginning of the barley harvest.

moments.title: “Whose young woman is this?”
moments.text: Ruth went out to glean, gathering the grain the harvesters left behind. “She happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz,” a relative of Naomi's husband. He asked his foreman, “Whose young woman is this?” He told her to stay in his field, close to his servant girls, and to drink from his men's jars. She bowed to the ground and asked why he should notice a foreigner. He had heard, he said, all she had done for her mother-in-law. At the meal he gave her roasted grain. Then he told his young men to pull stalks from the bundles and leave them for her. By evening she had about an ephah of barley. She carried it home to Naomi, with the food she had saved from her meal.

moments.title: At midnight
moments.text: Naomi wanted a home for Ruth. Boaz was one of their kinsman-redeemers, she said, and that night he was winnowing barley. She told Ruth to wash, put on perfume and her best clothes, and go down to the threshing floor. When he lay down, Ruth was to uncover his feet and lie down there. She did. At midnight Boaz woke with a start and found a woman at his feet. Ruth asked him to act as her kinsman-redeemer. He blessed her. There was a nearer redeemer, he said, but if that man would not, “as surely as the LORD lives, I will.” Before dawn he poured six measures of barley into her shawl and sent her home.

moments.title: The sandal
moments.text: Boaz sat down at the gate, called over the nearer kinsman and asked ten elders to sit with them. Naomi was selling Elimelech's land, he said. The man was ready to buy it back. But whoever bought it, Boaz added, must also take Ruth as his wife, to keep the dead man's name alive. The kinsman drew back: “I cannot redeem it myself, or I would jeopardize my own inheritance.” He took off his sandal, the old way of sealing a deal in Israel, and gave the right to Boaz. The elders blessed the marriage: “May the LORD make the woman entering your home like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel.”

moments.title: “A son has been born to Naomi”
moments.text: Boaz married Ruth, and “the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son.” The women of the town blessed the LORD, Who had not left Naomi without a redeemer. Naomi took the child on her lap and cared for him. The neighbour women named him Obed. “He became the father of Jesse, the father of David.” Centuries later, Matthew opened his Gospel with the family tree of Jesus. In it he wrote: “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth.”

words.note: Ruth wrote nothing. These are her words as her book records them. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

myths.claim: “Wherever you go, I will go” is a vow between lovers.
myths.truth: It is often read at weddings, but Ruth said it to her mother-in-law. Naomi was a widow with nothing to give her. She had just told Ruth to go back to her own mother's home and find a new husband in Moab. Ruth chose Naomi, her people and her God instead.

myths.claim: Ruth wept, homesick, in the fields of Bethlehem.
myths.truth: That picture comes from a poem, not the Bible. In his “Ode to a Nightingale”, in 1819, John Keats imagined the bird's song reaching “the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home, she stood in tears amid the alien corn.” In her book, Ruth weeps only on the road out of Moab. In Boaz's field she works “from morning until now”, and goes home with an ephah of barley.

cite.text: John Keats, “Ode to a Nightingale” (1819); Ruth 1:9-14; 2:7, 17

myths.claim: Ruth went to the threshing floor to seduce Boaz.
myths.truth: The book tells what she did and said, and no more. Naomi sent her, washed and perfumed, to lie down at his feet. When he woke, Ruth asked him to spread the corner of his garment over her, “for you are a kinsman-redeemer.” Ezekiel uses the same picture for God's covenant with Jerusalem: “I spread My cloak over you”. Boaz praised her kindness, promised to act that day, and sent her home before anyone could recognise her. Readers have long argued over how daring her visit was.

circle.name: Naomi
circle.text: Her mother-in-law, from Bethlehem. She lost her husband and both sons in Moab. Back home she planned Ruth's marriage, and took Ruth's son on her lap.

circle.name: Boaz
circle.text: A relative of Naomi's husband, “a prominent man of noble character”. He let her glean in his field, then redeemed the family's land and married her.

circle.name: Orpah
circle.text: Her sister-in-law, also from Moab. She kissed Naomi goodbye and went back “to her people and her gods”.

circle.name: Mahlon
circle.text: Her first husband, one of Naomi's two sons. He died in Moab. Only at the town gate does the book say which son she had married.

circle.name: Obed
circle.text: Her son by Boaz. The neighbour women named him, and he became the father of Jesse.

circle.name: Rahab
circle.text: Matthew names her as the mother of Boaz, which makes her Ruth's mother-in-law. Both women came from outside Israel, and they share one verse of Jesus' family tree.

circle.name: David
circle.text: Her great-grandson, the shepherd who became king. Her book ends with his name. When Saul hunted him, David asked the king of Moab to shelter his father and mother.

saint.big: The Orthodox honour her as a saint, **Righteous Ruth**, among the forefathers of Christ. Lutherans of the Missouri Synod keep her day on 16 July. The Catholic calendar has no day for her.

churches.note: Sunday of the Forefathers, in December
Named in Matthew's family tree of Jesus

paras: The OCA lists **Righteous Ruth**, the wife of Boaz, on the **Sunday of the Forefathers**, the Sunday between 11 and 17 December. On the **Sunday before the Nativity**, a week later, she is named again among the righteous women of the Old Testament.
Rome's 1916 book of martyrs does not name her either. The Church of England and the Episcopal Church keep no day for her.

kin.name: Abraham
kin.text: God told him to leave his country and his father's household. Boaz praised Ruth for doing the same: “you left your father and mother and the land of your birth”.

kin.name: Esther
kin.text: Hers is the only other book of the Bible named for a woman in every Christian Bible. Esther's story is set in a palace; Ruth's, in a barley field.

kin.name: Mary of Nazareth
kin.text: The last of the five women in Matthew's family tree of Jesus. Her Son was born in Bethlehem, Ruth's town.
